lessons.title: 80C Options Side by Side: Lock-In, Returns, Risk and Tax on Maturity

children.text: You now know every major 80C option on its own. Individually, each one sounds reasonable. The mistakes happen when you compare them the way brochures want you to: by the headline rate. This lesson lines them all up on the four measures that actually decide what you end up with: how long your money is locked, what it earns, how safe it is, and how much tax you pay on the way out.

body.text: Compare after tax, after lock-in and after risk. The headline rate is the least useful number on any brochure.

children.text: Lens 1: Tax on the Way Out

Every 80C option gets the same deduction on the way in. The difference is what happens after. Tax planners describe this with three letters, for the three points where tax can apply: when you invest, while it grows, and when you withdraw. E means exempt, T means taxed.

body.title: The Tax Framework of Each Option

cards.definition: PPF, SSY, and EPF within its limits. Deduction on entry, no tax on growth, no tax on withdrawal. The best possible treatment.
NSC, SCSS, Post Office TD and bank tax saver FDs. Deduction on entry, but interest is taxed every year as it is earned.
ELSS: deduction on entry, no yearly tax while invested, but gains above ₹1.25 lakh a year are taxed at 12.5% when you sell.
NPS: deduction on entry, no yearly tax, but only 60% of the corpus is tax-free at exit. The extra lump sum and annuity income are taxed.
Life insurance and ULIPs: tax-free payouts only if premium stays within 10% of sum assured and the yearly premium limits.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: NSC gives a deduction on entry, its interest is taxed every year, and the maturity amount is not taxed again. Its tax framework is ___.
body.explanation: Exempt on entry, taxed during accumulation, exempt on withdrawal: ETE. That middle T is why NSC's 7.7% shrinks so much for higher-slab taxpayers.

body.caption: For taxable options only. Use the effective yield for quarterly compounding: 7.5% compounded quarterly is 7.71% a year. Tax-free options keep their full rate.
Post-tax yearly return for guaranteed and government-set options (cess included, surcharge ignored)

body.title: Post-tax return for a 30% slab taxpayer

body.text: Notice how tax reshuffles the ranking. NSC's 7.7% beats PPF's 7.1% on paper, but after tax at 30%, PPF earns 1.8 percentage points more. SCSS's 8.2% matches SSY before tax and falls more than 2.5 points behind after it. For higher-slab taxpayers, EEE options almost always win among guaranteed choices.

body.title: Your Turn: Post-Tax SCSS
body.prompt: Mrs. Fernandes, 63, a retired nurse in Goa, is in the 20% slab on the old regime. What is her post-tax return on SCSS at 8.2%, including 4% cess? Enter the percentage to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Tax rate with cess = 20% × 1.04 = 20.8%. Post-tax return = 8.2% × (1 − 0.208) = 8.2% × 0.792 = 6.49%. On the old regime, the senior citizen interest deduction of up to ₹50,000 under Section 153 (80TTB) can push her effective return a little higher.

children.text: Lens 3: How Long Your Money Is Locked

EPF and NPS are not on the chart because they run until retirement, with partial withdrawals under specific conditions. A long lock-in is not bad in itself. It is only bad when it does not match the goal the money is meant for.

columns.label: Guaranteed or government-set
points: PPF, EPF, SSY, NSC, SCSS, Post Office TD, bank tax saver FD
Capital is safe; sovereign backing for most
Main risk: returns lag inflation after tax, especially for ETE options
Rates on PPF and SSY can be cut in future quarters
Suits safety-first money and short to medium goals

columns.label: Market-linked
points: Value can fall 20% to 40% in a bad year
Main risk: needing the money during a market fall
Historically higher long-term returns than fixed options
Suits long goals and investors who can hold through volatility

body.title: Spot the Weakest Choice
body.question: Divya, 35, is in the 30% slab on the old regime. She wants guaranteed returns and will need the money in exactly 5 years. Among the options she can use, which gives her the lowest post-tax return?
options: They all give the same post-tax return because they are all taxable
body.explanation: All three are taxable, but the starting rate still matters: NSC and the Post Office TD both work out to about 5.30% after tax at her slab, while the 6.50% bank FD gives about 4.58%. SCSS would beat all three but she is not eligible below 60, and PPF would beat them after tax but does not fit a 5-year need.

body.label: The same ₹1.5 lakh, very different outcomes
body.context: The gap between EPF's 8.25% tax-free and a bank tax saver FD's 4.58% after tax, for a 30% slab taxpayer. Both earn the identical 80C deduction.

body.title: Scenario: Three Constraints, One Gap
body.scenario: Aakash, 31, is a data engineer in Pune on the old regime, in the 30% slab. His EPF covers ₹72,000 of his 80C limit, leaving a ₹78,000 gap. He has three wishes: some of the money must stay completely safe, some should grow meaningfully over the long term, and he wants at least part of it accessible within about 5 years in case he starts an MBA.
body.prompt: Using the four lenses, propose how Aakash could split his ₹78,000 gap, and explain what each piece does.
body.modelAnswer: One reasonable split: about ₹30,000 in PPF, about ₹30,000 in ELSS through a monthly SIP, and about ₹18,000 in NSC. PPF is his safest and best post-tax guaranteed option at 7.1% tax-free, ideal for money he truly will not touch, with partial withdrawals from year 7 as a backstop. ELSS covers long-term growth; at 31 with a 30% slab, equity gains taxed at 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh a year are far more efficient than FD interest taxed at 31.2%, and each SIP instalment unlocks after 3 years if the MBA materialises. NSC gives a guaranteed, fixed 7.7% that matures in 5 years and can be pledged for a loan, so it lines up with the MBA timeline, though its interest is taxed. He should avoid the bank tax saver FD, which has the weakest post-tax return and no loan facility, and an endowment policy, which locks money longer for less. The exact percentages matter less than the logic: match each rupee to a purpose, then pick the option that is best after tax for that purpose.

body.title: Go Deeper: ELSS Return After Tax

children.text: Market-linked options do not fit neatly into a post-tax yield table because the tax depends on when you sell and your other gains. As an illustration: ₹1,50,000 in ELSS growing at an assumed 12% for 10 years becomes ₹4,65,877. The gain of ₹3,15,877 attracts tax of ₹24,814 after the ₹1,25,000 exemption. The post-tax value of ₹4,41,063 works out to about 11.4% a year.

content.caption: Assumes the full ₹1.25 lakh exemption is available in the year of sale and a constant 12% return, which markets never deliver in a straight line.

points: Every 80C option gives the same deduction; they differ on lock-in, return, risk and tax on the way out.
EEE options (EPF within limits, PPF, SSY) keep their full rate; ETE options (NSC, SCSS, TD, FD) lose a large chunk to yearly tax.
At the 30% slab, post-tax returns range from about 8.25% for EPF to about 4.58% for a bank tax saver FD.
ELSS has the shortest lock-in at 3 years but the highest risk; SSY has the longest commitment at 21 years.
Market-linked options have historically offered higher long-term returns, taxed only on sale and only above ₹1.25 lakh of gains a year.
Match each part of your 80C gap to a purpose, then choose the best post-tax option for that purpose.
